Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 1:

Surat al-Buruj

There is no disagreement that it is Meccan, nor that it has twenty-two verses. Its connection to what precedes it lies in its containing, like the one before it, the promise to the believers and the warning to the disbelievers, together with honouring the Qur'an and the magnificence of its status. In al-Bahr: when He, glory be to Him, mentioned that He is most knowing of what they plot against the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the believers, of deceit and trickery and harming those who had embraced Islam with kinds of harm such as beating, killing, crucifixion, burning with the sun, heating stones, and placing the bodies of those they wished to tempt upon it, He mentioned that this practice existed among the nations that came before, for they used to torture with fire, and that the tormented had such steadfastness in faith that it prevented them from returning from their religion, and that those who tortured them are cursed. Likewise, those of the disbelieving Quraysh who tortured the believers. So this surah is an admonition to the Quraysh and a reinforcement for those among the believers who are being tortured. End of quotation. This is a sound opinion.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sky containing the mansions of the stars﴾, i.e., the palaces, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. According to a group, what is meant by them is the well-known twelve constellations (buruj). The original sense of burj is a clear matter; then it became the literal term for a high palace, because it is visible to observers. Also, what rises above the wall of a city is called a burj. The "buruj of the sky" in the well-known sense, although they have become literal usage, are in origin a metaphor: they were likened to palaces for their height, and because the stars descend into them like their inhabitants. Thus there is an explicit metaphor followed by an implicit one. It was also said that the sky was likened to the wall of a city, and so buruj was ascribed to it. It was also said that they are the stations of the moon, and this returns to the first opinion, since the buruj are divided into twenty-eight stations, and the discussion of them has already passed. Mujahid, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah said: they are the stars.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, a hadith traced to the Prophet with the wording "the planets" (al-kawakib) instead of "the stars"; and Allah knows best its authenticity.

Ibn al-Mundhir and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih that he said: they are the great stars. On this view it is called buruj because of its manifestness, and likewise according to what precedes it, though manifestness differs; and it does not clearly include all the stars. It was also said: they are the gates of the sky, and they were so named because the descents of the angels, peace be upon them, come out from them, so they were likened to the palaces of great men from which decrees descend, or their commands come from them; or because, being the source of manifestness, they were described with it metaphorically in the other sense. It was said regarding the connection and the twelve buruj, in reality, according to what the authorities of the science of astronomy (hay'a) mention, that they are considered in the highest sphere called the sphere of spheres and the Atlas sphere, and they claimed that it is the Throne in the language of the Sharia. But since they were not visible to the senses, they indicated them by what corresponded to them at the time of dividing the highest sphere, from the known forms such as the Ram, the Bull and others, which are in the eighth sphere called by them the sphere of the fixed stars, and called the Kursi in the language of the Sharia, as they claimed. So the constellation of the Ram, for example, is merely one part of the twelve parts of the highest sphere, to which the form of the Ram among the fixed stars corresponded at the time of division; and the constellation of the Bull is merely one part of that, to which the form of the Bull corresponded at that time too, and so on. It is said "at the time of division" because every form has moved, though slowly, away from what it once corresponded to among those constellations, until the Ram nearly corresponds today to the constellation of the Bull, and the Bull to the constellation of Gemini, and so on. On this basis, and whether the intended buruj are the twelve buruj or the stations, it was said: the intended sky is the highest sphere; and it was said: the eighth sphere, because the forms indicating the buruj appear in it, and for this reason it is called the sphere of the buruj. It was also said: the lowest heaven, because they are seen in it by plain sense perception, analogous to what was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾. It was also said: the genus encompassing every heaven, because the heavens are transparent, so the upper share in what is in the lower, since it is seen in them clearly. When the buruj are taken to mean the stars, it was said: the intended sky is the eighth sphere, because they are in it in reality; and it was said: the lowest heaven; and it was said: the genus in the manner mentioned. It is not intended, as some said, the Atlas sphere, I mean the highest sphere, since, as its name indicates, it has no stars. When the gates are intended, it was said: the intended sky is everything other than the sphere of spheres, called in the language of the Sharia the Throne, for it has not been reported that it has gates. Know that most of what has been mentioned is based on the words of the ancient astronomers, and it has no basis in the Sharia, and one scarcely hears in it the application of the word "sky" to the Throne or the Kursi. But when some Islamic thinkers heard from the philosophers of nine spheres and wished to apply that to what is narrated in the Sharia, they claimed that seven of them are the seven heavens, and the two remaining are the Kursi and the Throne; and they did not realise that there are reports which reject that, and whether the rational proof requires it is a matter for discussion, as is not hidden. As for one who returns to the words of the modern astronomers and considers their proofs for what they say about the heavenly bodies and the manner of their arrangement, he will find strength in what the earlier scholars held on this; so what should be said is: the buruj are the stations for the stars absolutely, which the elite and the common people observe, and it does not matter in which sky they are, or the stars themselves wherever they are, or the gates of the sky mentioned in the language of the Sharia and the authentic hadiths, and these are for every heaven, and nothing of them has been established for the Throne or the Kursi. The sky is intended as its genus, or the lowest heaven in other than the last opinion, as you have heard before. So do not be heedless.

ومن ﴿وَالْيَوْمِ الْمَوْعُودِ﴾ أي: الموعود به، وهو يوم القيامة باتفاق المفسرين. وقيل: لعله اليوم الذي يخرج الناس فيه من قبورهم، فقد قال سبحانه: ﴿يَخْرُجُونَ مِنَ الْأَجْدَاثِ سِرَاعًا كَأَنَّهُمْ إِلَىٰ نُصُبٍ يُوفِضُونَ﴾ ﴿خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ تَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ ذَٰلِكَ الْيَوْمُ الَّذِي كَانُوا يُوعَدُونَ﴾ أو ﴿يَوْمَ نَطْوِي السَّمَاءَ كَطَيِّ السِّجِلِّ لِلْكُتُبِ﴾. وقيل: يمكن أن يُراد به يوم شفاعة النبي ﷺ، على ما أشار إليه قوله تعالى: ﴿عَسَىٰ أَن يَبْعَثَكَ رَبُّكَ مَقَامًا مَحْمُودًا﴾. ولا يخفى أن جميع ذلك داخل في يوم القيامة.

[Page 87]

﴿And a witness and a witnessed﴾: that is, whoever bears witness to that Day and attends it from among the created beings raised therein, and what is witnessed therein of its terrors and wonders. Thus Allah, glory be to Him, has sworn by the Day of Resurrection and what occurs in it, to magnify that Day and to instil dread in those who deny it. The indefiniteness of the two descriptions is for magnification, meaning: "and a witness and a witnessed whose description cannot be grasped," or for multiplicity, as was said regarding ﴿a soul shall know what it has brought forth﴾.

Al-Tirmidhi and a group [of compilers] narrated from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The witness is the Day of Friday (Yawm al-Jumu'a), and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafa." This is also related from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, may Allah be pleased with them both, likewise traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). A group [of narrators] also transmitted it from Ali, may Allah honour his face, and others among the Companions and the Successors (tabi'un).

Al-Hakim transmitted it, and declared it sound, from Abu Hurayra, also traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The witness is the Day of 'Arafa and the Day of Friday, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ali, may Allah honour his face: "The witness is the Day of Friday, and the witnessed is the Day of the Star (Yawm al-Najm)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Hasan ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both and honour their faces, that a man asked him about this. He said: "Have you asked anyone before me?" He said: "Yes. I asked Ibn Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr, and they said: 'The Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Dhabh) and the Day of Friday.'" He said: "No, but the witness is Muhammad." In another narration [it is said]: "[He is] the grandfather of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Then he recited: ﴿And We bring you as a witness over these people﴾, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. Then he recited: ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾.

Al-Nasa'i and a group [of compilers] narrated by various routes from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, something similar. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "The witness is Allah, mighty and majestic, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection."

From Mujahid, Ikrima and Ata ibn Yasar: "The witness is Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection."

From Ibn al-Musayyib: "The witness is the Day of Tarwiya (8th of Dhu al-Hijja), and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafa."

From al-Tirmidhi: "The witness is the guardian angels (al-Hafaza), and the witnessed (i.e., the one witnessed against) is: the people."

From Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya: "They are the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his community (ummah), peace be upon him." And also from him: "They are the Prophets, peace be upon them, and their nations."

From Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil: "They are the limbs and their owners."

It was also said: "They are the Day of Monday and the Day of Friday." It was said: "They are the angels who follow one another (al-Mutaʿaqibun), peace be upon them, and the Dawn Recitation (Qur'an al-Fajr)." It was said: "They are the star, the night and the day." It was said: "The witness is Allah, exalted, and the angels and people of knowledge (Ulu al-ʿIlm), and the witnessed to is the Oneness [of Allah], and that religion with Allah is Islam." It was said: "The witness is His created beings, exalted, and the witnessed to is the Oneness [of Allah]." It was said: "They are the Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad) and the pilgrims (al-Hujjaj)." It was said: "They are the nights, the days and the children of Adam."

From al-Hasan: "There is no day but that it calls out: 'I am a new day, and I am a witness over what is done in me, so make use of me; for if my sun sets, you will not reach me until the Day of Resurrection.'"

It was said: "[They are] the nation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and all the other nations."

It is permissible that the two terms refer to the Muqarrabun (those brought near) and the ʿIlliyyun (the highest of the high), based on His saying, exalted: ﴿It is a written record﴾ ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾. And that the witness refers to the child who said: "O mother, be patient; for you are upon the truth," as will come, Allah willing.

The witnessed-for is his mother and the believers, because if his mother was upon the truth, then the rest of the believers are likewise.

It was said: "All the sayings on this matter, as far as I have come upon them, number about thirty sayings." The description, according to some of them, is from shahada in the sense of presence, the opposite of absence; and according to others, it is from shahada as testimony against adversaries. The first of these is the testimony of the limbs, by Allah making them speak, the One who made everything speak. Likewise the Black Stone; and there is no remoteness in its presence on the Day of Resurrection to testify for the pilgrims. As for the testimony of the Day itself, it is possible that it occurs after it manifests in a form, like the manifestation of the Qur'an in the form of a pale man who meets its companion when he rises from his grave, and the manifestation of death in the form of a ram on the Day of Resurrection, until it is slaughtered between Paradise and Hell, and other such matters.

Al-Shihab [al-Alusi] said: "Allah is capable of bringing the Day into presence to bear witness, and He did not explain the manner of this. If it is as we have mentioned, then so be it. If it is something else, namely that the Day itself is present on that Day, then it apparently follows that time would have a time; and although whoever permits it among the theologians does permit it, there is obscurity in testimony by the tongue of speech regarding it. Similar to it is the calling of the Day that you heard just now from al-Hasan, if it is also by the tongue of speech rather than the tongue of state, as is the more likely in my view."

Abu Hayyan chose from among the sayings, on the assumption that shahada is meant in the second sense, the view that the witness is one who bears witness on that Day, namely the promised Day of Resurrection, and that the witnessed is one against whom testimony is given therein. And on the assumption that shahada is meant in the first sense, the view that the witness is the created beings present for the reckoning, and the witnessed is the Day. Perhaps the repetition of the oath by it, although the title differs, is for the increase of its magnification, so reflect.

The response to the oath: it was said that it is His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted﴾. Al-Mubarrad said it is His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe﴾. Ibn Jurayj stated this explicitly. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud what indicates it. And more than one said: it is

**[Page 88]**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Killed were the companions of the trench﴾. The *lam* is omitted from it because of its length, and the original is *la-qutila* (the *lam* of emphasis with *qutila*), as in his saying:

*I swore to her by Allah an oath of a sinner: they slept, so there is neither talk nor one awake.*

It was also said: the omission is of the *lam* and *qad* together, and the original is *la-qad qutila*. This is based on what is well known, that the affirmative, inflected (*mutasarrif*, a verb that takes the full range of forms) past verb whose object has not been placed before it must be accompanied by *lam* and *qad*, and that it is not permitted to drop one of them except when the speech is long, as in His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ after His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, and so on, and in the verse mentioned. It is not permitted to posit the *lam* without *qad*, because it does not enter upon a past verb that is free of it. The full discussion belongs in its proper place, as in the commentaries on *al-Tashil* (*Sharh al-Tashil*) and others. In any case, the sentence is declarative.

Some verifying scholars said: the more evident view is that it is supplicatory (*du'a'iyyah*), indicating the response, as if it were said: "I swear by these things that the disbelievers of Quraysh are indeed cursed and deserving that it be said of them, 'They have been killed,' as is the case with the companions of the trench." This is because the surah was revealed to strengthen the believers in the faith they hold, to make them patient against the harm of the disbelievers, and to remind them of what happened to those before them, of the torment inflicted on the people of faith and their patience through it, so that they might take comfort in them, endure what they suffered from their people, and know that they are like those (companions of the trench) before Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, in being cursed and driven away. So "killing" here is an expression for the utmost curse and expulsion, since supplication from Him, may He be glorified, in its literal sense is impossible. Thus its necessary implication is intended: wrath and being driven away from His mercy, may He be majestic and exalted.

Others said: the more evident view is that it should be understood as: "Indeed they are to be killed, just as the companions of the trench were killed." This would then be a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ) of the killing of the arrogant disbelievers, to raise his religion, and it would be a miracle through the killing of their leaders at the Battle of Badr. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of this is to keep "killing" in its literal sense and to take the sentence as declarative, and it is, as you see, far from convincing.

It is reported in *al-Bahr* that the response is omitted, and that its estimated form is: "You will certainly be resurrected," or the like, but this is nothing, as is not hidden.

*Al-Ukhdud* (the trench) means a ditch, a cleft in the earth or the like, built, and it carries the meaning of *al-khaqq* and *al-ukhquq* (a long narrow hole or fissure). From it is what came in the report about Suraqah, when he pursued the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his horse's legs sank into the *akhaqiq* (fissures) of jerboas, that is, the legs of his horse sank into the holes of jerboas.

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others reported from the hadith of Suhayb, who raised it (to the Prophet ﷺ): "There was a king among the kings, and this king had a soothsayer who foretold for him. That soothsayer said to him: 'Look for me a clever boy, and I will teach him this knowledge of mine, for I fear that I may die and this knowledge will be cut off from you, and there will be no one among you who knows it.' So they searched for a boy as he described, and they ordered him to attend that soothsayer and to go to him regularly. The boy began to go to him, and on the boy's path there was a monk in a hermitage. Whenever the boy passed by him, he would ask that monk, and he continued with him until the monk told him, and he said: 'I only worship Allah, may He be exalted.' The boy began to remain with the monk and to be late for the soothsayer, so the soothsayer sent to the boy's family, saying, 'He hardly comes to me.' The boy told the monk of this, and the monk said to him: 'When the soothsayer says to you, "Where were you?" say, "With my family," and when your family says to you, "Where were you?" tell them that you were with the soothsayer.' While the boy was in that state, he passed by a large crowd of people who had been held up by an animal, said to have been a lion. The boy took a stone and said: 'O Allah, if what the monk says is true, I ask You that I kill this animal, and if what the soothsayer says is true, I ask You that I do not kill it.' Then he threw and killed the animal. The people said: 'Who killed it?' They said: 'The boy.' The people were terrified and said: 'This boy has knowledge that no one has ever possessed.' Then a blind man heard of this, came to him and said: 'If you restore my sight, then for you is such-and-such.' The boy said: 'I do not want that from you, but tell me: if your sight returns to you, will you believe in the One who restored it to you?' He said: 'Yes.' So the boy restored his sight, and the blind man believed. The king heard of their affair, sent for them, brought them and said: 'I will certainly kill each one of you with a killing by which I will not kill his companion.' So he ordered the monk and the man who had been blind to be brought, and the saw was placed on the middle of the head of one of them, and it killed him, and he killed the other with another kind of killing. Then he ordered the boy and said: 'Take him to such-and-such mountain and throw him down from its top.' They took him to that mountain, and when they reached the place from which they intended to throw him, they began to fall off that mountain and to tumble down until none of them remained except the boy. Then the boy returned, and the king ordered that they take him to the sea and throw him into it. He was taken to the sea, but Allah, may He be exalted, scattered those who were with him and saved him. The boy said to the king: 'You will not kill me until you crucify me, shoot me, and say: "In the name of Allah, Lord of the boy."' So he ordered him to be crucified, then shot him and said: 'In the name of Allah, Lord of the boy.' The boy placed his hand on his temple when he was shot, then died. The people said: 'This boy has indeed known a knowledge that no one else has known; for we believe in the Lord of this boy.' It was said to the king: 'Are you in distress if three people oppose you? Here is the whole world that has opposed you.' So he dug a trench, put firewood and fire in it, then gathered the people and said: 'Whoever turns back from his religion, we will leave him alone, and whoever does not turn back, we will throw him into this fire.' So he began throwing them into that trench." He (the narrator) said: "Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Killed were the companions of the trench﴾ until He reached: ﴿the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾."

And in it: "As for the boy, he was buried, then he was exhumed, and it is mentioned that he came out during the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, with his finger on his temple just as he had placed it when he was killed." And in some of its narrations: "A woman came with a small son of hers, as if she hesitated to fall into the fire, so the child said: 'O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth.'"

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abd Allah ibn Nujayy, who said: "I witnessed Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, when the bishop of Najran came to him and asked him about the companions of the trench, and he related the story to him. Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, said: 'I know more about them than you do. A prophet from Abyssinia was sent to his people.'" Then he (Ali), may Allah be pleased with him, recited: ﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you; of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you﴾. "He called them, and the people followed him. He fought them, and his companions were killed, and he was taken and bound, but he escaped. Some men took to him and he fought them, and they were killed, and he was taken and bound. So they dug a trench, put fires in it, and began to present the people; whoever followed the Prophet was thrown into it, and whoever followed them was left alone. A woman came last among those who came, and with her was a child. She hesitated, so the child said: 'O mother, be patient and do not doubt,' and she fell."

Abd ibn Humayd reported from him, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "The Magians were a people of a Book, and they held firmly to their Book, and wine had been made lawful for them. One of their kings drank from it, and it overcame his reason, so he took his sister or his daughter and had intercourse with her. When the intoxication left him, he regretted it and said to her: 'Woe to you, what is this that I have done, and what is the way out of it?' She said: 'The way out of it is that you address the people and say: "O people, Allah, may He be exalted, has made lawful the marrying of sisters or daughters."' The people, their whole community, said: 'We seek refuge in Allah, may He be exalted, from believing in this or acknowledging it. Has a prophet brought it, or has it been revealed to us in a Book?' He returned to his companion and said: 'Woe to you, the people have refused me in this.' She said: 'If they refuse you, then spread the whip among them.' He spread the whip among them, but they refused to acknowledge it. She said: 'Then draw the sword against them.' They refused to acknowledge it. She said: 'Then dig a trench for them and kindle fires in it. Whoever follows you, leave him alone.' So he dug a trench for them, kindled fires in it, and presented the people of his realm with this; whoever refused, he threw into the fire, and whoever did not refuse, he left alone." It was also said: "A man who had been of the religion of Jesus, peace be upon him, came to Najran, and they answered him. Dhu Nuwas the Jew marched against them with troops from Himyar, and he gave them the choice between the fire and Judaism. They refused, so he burned of them twelve thousand in the trenches." It was said: "Seventy thousand." It is mentioned that the length of the trench was forty cubits and its width twelve cubits. Because the reports about the story differ, they differed about the location of the trench: it was said to be in Najran, due to this last report, and it was said to be in the land of Abyssinia, due to the earlier report of Ibn Nujayy.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah, from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that it was at *Midhra' al-Yaman*, that is, its villages. This does not contradict its being in Najran, because Najran is a town in Yemen.

Likewise they differed about the companions of the trench, so more than ten opinions have been related about them, among them that they were Abyssinians, and among them that they were of the Nabataeans, which was narrated from Ikrimah, and among them that they were of the Children of Israel, which was narrated from Ibn Abbas. The most sound of the narrations in the story, in my view, is what we have already mentioned from Suhayb, may Allah be pleased with him, and reconciliation is possible. Isam al-Din said: "Perhaps all that has been narrated has occurred, and the Qur'an encompasses it, so do not be heedless."

Al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam read: *qutthila* with doubling (tashdid), and this is an intensification in cursing them because of the magnitude of what they committed. The Prophet (ﷺ), as Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Awf, and Abd ibn Humayd from al-Hasan, used to seek refuge from the severity of affliction whenever the companions of the trench were mentioned.

﴿The fire﴾ is a *badal ishtimal* (a "comprehensive" or inclusive apposition) to *al-Ukhdud* (the trench), and the connecting pronoun is understood: that is, "in it," or the noun is put in the place of the pronoun, or because its connection to the trench is known, it does not need a connecting pronoun. The same applies to anything whose connection is evident from what precedes it. Abu Hayyan permitted it to be a *badal kull min kull* (a "whole-for-whole" apposition) with an elided element, that is, "the trench of the fire," but this is not the right view. Some readers recited *al-nar* ("the fire") in the nominative. It is said that this means "the fire killed them," as in His saying ﴿He is glorified therein in the mornings and evenings﴾ and ﴿men﴾, according to the reading *yusabbaḥu* in the passive voice, and as in the line:

*Let Yazid the suppliant weep for a dispute,*

and the people of the trench would then be the believers. The meaning of "killed" here is not cursing. It is also permitted that they be the disbelievers, and that the killing be literal, based on what al-Rabi' ibn Anas, al-Kalbi, Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu Ishaq said: that God sent a wind upon the believers which seized their souls, and the fire came out and burned the disbelievers who were on the two edges of the trench. You know that the saying of these men contradicts the saying of the majority and what the narratives they mentioned indicate, so it should not be relied upon. Taking "killed" in its literal sense is also not suitable to the context. Perhaps the better way to explain this reading is that *al-nar* ("the fire") is the predicate of an elided subject, that is, "it is" or "he is the fire," and the pronoun refers back to the trench. Describing it as the fire comes as an exaggeration, as if it were the very essence of fire.

﴿possessing the fuel﴾ is a description of it, expressing its greatness, the height of its flames, and the abundance of what it requires. The reason it conveys this is that He did not say "kindled" but made it "possessing fuel," that is, its owner. This is a metaphor for its excessive increase, because of the abundance of what its flame is raised by, which is the wood with which it is kindled, since the definite article here is for totality. When it owns every piece of wood with which it is fed, its burning and its flame become great. This does not mean that one says *dhū kadhā* ("possessor of such-and-such") only of someone who has much of such-and-such, because this is not established. *Dhū al-nūn* ("the one of the fish") rules this out, and likewise *dhū al-'arsh* ("the Lord of the Throne").

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Haywah and Isa read *al-wuqūd* with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, which is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), unlike the form with a *fatḥa*, which denotes what is kindled with. Sibawayh has related that it is a verbal noun like its meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 6:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they were sitting over it﴾
Page 90
It is an adverbial clause of time (zarf) modifying "qutila" (was cursed/killed); that is, they were cursed at the time when they surrounded the fire, sitting around it in a place close to it, overlooking it from the edges of the trench (ukhdud), as in the verse of al-A'sha:

It is kindled for two shivering men who warm themselves at it, while dew and the one who shaves his head (al-Muhallaq) spend the night beside the fire.

It has also been said that the statement contains an implied noun (taqdir mudaf): that is, "over its edges" or something similar. But the majority hold that the intended meaning is that without any such implied element.

﴿And they are witnesses to what they do to the believers.﴾ That is: some of them will bear witness for others before the King that none of them fell short in what he was commanded. Or they will bear witness before Him to the goodness of what they did and its being founded on righteousness, as has been said. Or some of them will testify against others about that abominable deed on the Day of Resurrection. Or they will testify against themselves to that on the Day when their own limbs bear witness to their deeds.

It has been said that "ʿalā" (on) here means "maʿa" (with), and the meaning is: they are present, together with what they do to the believers of torment, not softened toward them because of the extreme hardness of their hearts. As for one who claims that God, exalted is He, saved the believers and that He only burned the disbelievers, he says here: the meaning is "and they are witnesses to what they intend to do to the believers." In any case, there is taghlib (a figure of speech in which one group is given precedence over another) in "the believers," and what is meant is the believing men and the believing women. Among the strange views that are not to be paid heed is what has been said: that the People of the Trench were ʿAmr ibn Hind, known as Muharriq, and those with him, who burned a hundred men of Banu Tamim. The pronoun in "and they are witnesses to what they do" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, who used to persecute the believing men and women.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 8:

﴿And they did not take revenge on them﴾, i.e., they did not disapprove of them or find fault with them. In the Mufradat of al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani's lexicon of Qur'anic vocabulary) it is said: "naqimtu al-shay'" means that I disapproved of the thing with my tongue or with punishment. Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah and others read ﴿نِقِمُوا﴾ with a kasra on the qaf. The clause is coordinated with the nominal clause before it, and what made this acceptable, as it is said, is that the nominal clause falls within the scope of ʾidh (when), which is followed by a past-tense verb, so the coordination is of a verbal clause upon a verbal clause. It is also said that this verbal clause is to be understood as: "and they did not take revenge on them."

﴿Except that they believe in God, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾: this is an exception that makes clear their innocence of anything that is blamed or disapproved of at all, following the pattern of the poet's words:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of battalions."

That unbelievers regard faith as a disapproved matter, while the poet does not regard the notches on swords as such, does not harm the point, in my view, since the mention of this by the Exalted and Majestic One follows that same pattern of emphasizing praise through something resembling blame. Moreover, if the people were polytheists, what they disapproved of was not faith in God, Exalted is He, but the negation of all other objects of their false worship; and if they were deniers of the divine attributes (mu'attilah), what they disapproved of was nothing but the affirmation of a deity unknown to them. But since the outcome of both is the denial of the true God, who is described with the attributes of majesty and honour, He expressed it with what has been mentioned, making clear what you have heard, so reflect. Some scholars have made a statement on this point which al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) rejected; if you wish to see it, return to it. In al-Muntakhab it is said: the Exalted only said ﴿Except that they believe﴾ because the punishment was in fact directed at faith in the future; had they disbelieved in it, they would not have been punished for what had passed. So it is as if He, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Except that they persist in their faith." End of quote.

It seems that he understood naqam as punishment for disapproval, and his description of Him, Mighty and Majestic, as "the Mighty" means the Dominant whose punishment is to be feared, and "the Praiseworthy" means the Bountiful whose reward is to be hoped for, and the confirmation of this by His, Exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 9:

﴿Whose is the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ This is to indicate the basis (manat) of their faith.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾ is a promise for them and a warning for those who tormented them. The knowledge of Allah, majestic is His affair, which encompasses the attributes of majesty and beauty, regarding all things, among which are the deeds of both groups, necessitates the full recompense of each of them. And since it is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for that, and what is fitting for it is independence, the noble Name is used here instead of a pronoun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾ That is, they tested them in their religion so that they would turn back from it. The intended meaning of "those who persecuted" and of "the believing men and believing women" is the persecuted, namely specifically the People of the Trench and those thrown into it, or in a more general sense. The people mentioned enter into it in a primary way, and this is the more apparent. It has also been said that the intended referent of the relative clause is the disbelievers of Quraysh, who tortured the believing men and believing women of this community with various kinds of torment. As for His, exalted is He, saying ﴿then they did not repent﴾, Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What strengthens that the verse refers to Quraysh is that this expression applies to them more firmly than to those about whom it is known that they died upon their disbelief. As for Quraysh, among them at the time of its revelation were those who repented and believed. You know that this, as it stands, does not undermine the apparent generality." The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is ﴿then they did not repent﴾ from their persecution. ﴿For them is the punishment of Hell﴾, that is, because of that persecution of theirs.

﴿And for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾, and it is another fire of greater burning, as the form fa'il indicates, because of their not repenting and their indifference to what had proceeded from them. Some of the eminent scholars said: That is, ﴿for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ because of their disbelief, for such an act is not conceivable from anyone other than a disbeliever; ﴿and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ because of their persecution of the believing men and believing women. And in making that the recompense of the persecutions there is a beauty that is not hidden.

It was objected that the title of disbelief was not explicitly stated in the relative clause; what is explicitly stated is the persecutions and the non-repentance. So the more apparent view is to take these two as two causes, in order, in the consequent clause. It has also been said: That is, ﴿for them is Hell﴾ in the Hereafter and ﴿for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ in this world, based on what was narrated from al-Rabi', and whoever you heard that the fire turned back upon them and burned them, you know its condition. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that ﴿then they did not repent﴾ rejects it, because those burners were not reported to us as having repented; rather the apparent view is that they were not cursed except that they had died upon disbelief. There is consideration in this. Upon this, the phrase ﴿and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ was delayed only for the sake of the rhyme endings (fawasil), or for completion and pairing; as if it were said: that, which is the greatest punishment, is certainly going to occur, and this too they will not get beyond. In al-Kashf: The correct view is that the punishment of Hell and the punishment of the Burning are one; it is described with what indicates that they are utterly distanced from His mercy, the Mighty, the Majestic, and that it is a punishment which is purely burning, and that is the intense scorching, and sufficient is it as a punishment. The apparent view is that he treated "the Burning" as a verbal noun, and the idafah as explicative, and there is no harm in that, except that the unity he claimed is contrary to the apparent sense of the conjunction. Some of them said: If it were made a conjunction of the specific over the general for emphasis on it, it would be closer, since the punishment of Hell is by the bitter cold, burning, and other things; and perhaps what we have mentioned is further from dispute and debate.

The clause ﴿for them is the punishment of﴾ and so on occurs as the predicate of inna, or the prepositional phrase is the predicate, and "punishment" is raised by it as the subject, which is the best view; and the fa' is because of the meaning of a conditional in the subject; and its abrogation by inna does no harm, even though al-Akhfash claimed it. The verse has been cited, in some of its aspects, as evidence that the punishment of the disbelievers is multiplied by the sins that accompany it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ — without restriction, whether among those who were tested or others — ﴿for them﴾ — by reason of what has been mentioned of faith and righteous action — ﴿are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. If by the gardens (jannat) are meant the trees, then the flowing of the rivers beneath them is evident. If by them is meant the land that encompasses them, then "beneath" (tahtiyya) is with regard to its apparent part, since its trees cover its expanse, as the name "Jannah" (garden) indicates. As for separating the clause (fasl al-jumla), it has been said: it is because it serves as an emphasis for what the previous verse implied, namely the restriction of punishment to those who tormented the believing men and believing women and then did not repent. ﴿That﴾ is a reference to the fact that what has been mentioned is theirs and that they possess it. It has also been said that it refers to the described gardens, and the masculine form is used because it is interpreted as what has been mentioned, and because of what it contains of the sense of distance, to signal the loftiness of the rank and the remoteness of the station in excellence and honor. Its position is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is: ﴿the great triumph﴾, in comparison with which the triumph of this world and what it holds of desirable things becomes small. "Fawz" (triumph) is deliverance from evil and attainment of good. So according to the second view regarding the reference, it is a verbal noun (masdar) used to mean the object (maf'ul) for emphasis, while according to the first view it is a verbal noun retaining its own sense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), announcing that the disbelievers of his people have a full share of its meaning, as indicated by the mention of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his (ﷺ) pronoun. Al-batsh (the seizing) is taking with force and violence. Since it is described as severe (shadid), it has been multiplied and intensified; it is the seizing of Him, glorified and exalted, of the tyrants and the wrongdoers, and His taking them, glorified is He, with punishment and retribution.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats.﴾ That is: indeed, He, Mighty and Majestic, is the One who originates creation by bringing it into being, and He, glorified is He, repeats it by resurrection on the Day of Resurrection, as Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said. Or [it means]: He originates all that is originated and repeats all that is repeated, as Ibn Abbas said, without anyone having any intervention in either of them. And whoever is like this, his seizing (al-batsh) is in the utmost severity.

Page 92
Or [it means]: He initiates the seizing of the disbelievers in this world, then repeats it in the Hereafter. On both interpretations, the sentence is in the position of giving a reason (ta'lil) for what preceded.

Its aspect according to the second [interpretation] is clear, and according to the first we have already pointed to it. It was said: its aspect according to it is that repetition is for requital, so it includes seizing, but this is not the case. And it is related from Ibn Abbas: He initiates the punishment upon the disbelievers and repeats it upon them, so the Fire consumes them until they become charcoal, then Mighty and Majestic He repeats them as a new creation. In this there is obscurity, although the matter of the sentence according to it is most apparent. The use of yubdi'u (initiates) together with yu'id (repeats) is good, even though it has never been heard [alone in this combination], as has been explained in its proper place. Abu Zayd related that it was recited: "yabda'u" from bada'a in its triliteral form, and this is what is heard, but recitation with it is shadhdh (irregular/anomalous).

**﴿He is the Forgiving﴾** toward whomever He wills of the believers. It was also said: toward those who repent and believe. The restriction, according to those who hold the view of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah), is either due to the fitting of the context of warning, or because of the intensiveness in the form *al-Ghafur* (الغَفُور). The basic forgiveness does not depend on repentance, and its increase through repentance is known only to God Most High, for those who repent.

**﴿The Loving﴾** (al-Wadud): the one who loves greatly those who obey Him. Thus *fa'ul* (فَعُولٌ) is an intensive form of the active participle *al-wadd* (الوادّ). God's love and affection toward His creation is through His bounty and generosity, glory be to Him, and exalted be His majesty. From this, *al-Wadud* has been interpreted as "the one of abundant goodness." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means the one who shows affection to His servants, exalted be His majesty, through forgiveness. It was also said that *fa'ul* (فَعَوْلٌ) here carries the sense of *maf'ul* (مَفْعُولٌ), as in *rakub* (rideable) and *halub* (milkable); i.e., His righteous servants love Him, glory be to Him. This is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Al-Mubarrad related from al-Qadi Isma'il ibn Ishaq that *al-Wadud* is the one who has no child, and he cited the verse:

*And I ride into the clamor of battle upon a bare-backed mare, docile at the bit, a milch-camel and one who has no young.*

That is, she has no offspring toward which she yearns. Interpreting it in this sense alongside *al-Ghafur* is not appropriate, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 15:

﴿Owner of the Throne﴾: that is, its possessor. What is meant is its owner or its creator, and it is the greatest of created things.

From ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face: "If the waters of this world were gathered and poured over the surface of the Throne that is nearest to us, only a little of it would be covered."

The reports have come concerning its greatness to a degree that dazzles the minds. Al-Qaffāl said: ﴿Owner of the Throne﴾ means the owner of dominion and authority, as if he made "the Throne" a metaphor and figure of speech for dominion. It is also permitted that the Throne remain in its literal sense, and that "Owner of the Throne" mean the King, since the owner of a throne is none other than a king. Ibn ʿĀmir, in one transmission, read "ḏhī al-ʿarsh" with a yāʾ (ḏhī), on the basis that it is an attribute of "Rabbika" (your Lord). In that case, his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, He it is﴾ and so on, is a parenthetical clause, and the separation it causes does not harm the link between the attribute and the thing described; likewise, separating them by the predicate of the subject does no harm, since it is not foreign, for the described noun here is part of the subject. Ibn Mālik said in al-Tashīl: "It is permissible to separate the follower from the followed by that which does not wholly alienate it." Yet Ibn al-Ḥājib said: "Separating the attribute from the described noun by the predicate of the subject is anomalous, as in the verse:

And every brother from whom his brother parts, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads."

﴿The Glorious﴾: great in His essence, mighty and exalted, and in His attributes, glory be to Him, for He, exalted is His majesty, is necessarily existent, of complete power and perfect wisdom. Al-Ḥasan, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Ibn Waththāb, al-Aʿmash, al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim, and the two brothers (al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza) read "al-Majīdi" with a kasra as an attribute of "al-ʿArsh" (the Throne). Its glory (majd) is its loftiness, its greatness, and the beauty of its form and composition, for it has been said that the Throne is the most beautiful of bodies in form and composition. It is not part of its glory that the temporal events of existence occur through the mediation of its positions, as the astrologers claim, for that is false both by revelation and by reason, according to what their own principles require. On the reading "ḏhī al-ʿarsh" with a yāʾ, it is permissible for it to be an attribute of "ḏhī," and it has been permitted that it be an attribute of "Rabbika" (your Lord); but this is not the case, because the basic principle is the absence of separation between follower and followed, so one should not say so unless it is definitively required.

Page 93

﴿Accomplisher of whatever He wills﴾, such that nothing He wills, whether among His own acts, glorified is He, or the acts of others, mighty and majestic is He, escapes His will. The ﴿مَا﴾ (ma, "whatever") is for generality, and the indefiniteness of ﴿فَعَّالٌ﴾ carries a magnificence that is not hidden. This is also a clear refutation of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school that held that God's will is limited to what is good), who say that He wills the faith of the disbeliever and the obedience of the disobedient, yet these two escape His will. All the predicates, according to what Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi, the Qur'an commentator) found preferable, are predicates of ﴿هُوَ﴾ in His saying, ﴿He is the Forgiving﴾. It is also permitted that ﴿the Loving﴾, ﴿Owner of the Throne﴾, and ﴿the Glorious﴾ are attributes of "Forgiving." Whoever does not permit multiple predicates for a single subject holds that view, or assumes separate subjects for the things mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari (the Mu'tazili exegete, author of al-Kashshaf) stated without qualification that ﴿Accomplisher﴾ is a predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "He is Accomplisher." The author of al-Kashf (Sahib al-Kashf, al-Tibi) said: "He did not take it as a predicate of the preceding subject, namely ﴿He﴾ in His saying, ﴿He is the Forgiving﴾, because His saying, ﴿Accomplisher of whatever He wills﴾, confirms the two attributes: the seizing of enemies and the forgiving and love toward the friends. Had it been taken that way, this subtlety would have been lost." And this is a fine and precise observation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 17:

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Has the story of the hosts reached you?﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), in which there is an affirmation that Allah, Exalted is He, is One who does what He wills, and likewise of the severity of His seizing (bat'h), glorified is He, of the wrongdoing disobedient ones and the disbelieving tyrants. It is also a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by informing him that He will strike the disbelievers of his people with what befell the hosts. "Junud" (hosts) is the plural of "jund," which is said of an army (al-'askar), by way of comparison with "al-jund," meaning hard ground (al-ardh al-ghaliza), and likewise of helpers (a'wan). It is also said of a distinct category of creation, and likewise of every gathered group. What is meant by ﴿the hosts﴾ here is the groups who banded together against the prophets of Allah, peace be upon them, and gathered to harm them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 18:

﴿Pharaoh and Thamud﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the hosts﴾, a substitute of the whole for the whole, through the omission of a modifier (mudaf): that is, the hosts of Pharaoh. Or it is intended that by Pharaoh is meant he and his people, and his people were dispensed with by mentioning him, because they are his followers. It has been said: the substitute is the whole group, not each of the two conjoined nouns, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Al-Samin said: it is permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by "a'ni" (I mean), because when it does not agree with what precedes it, it must be cut off (qat'). This was objected to on the grounds that it would then be an explanation (tafsir) of "the hosts", and the problem returns. It was answered that the thing explained in that case is the whole group, and considering it together with "a'ni" is not like considering it together with substitution (ibdal). The meaning of "their account" is what proceeded from them of persistence in disbelief and error, and what befell them of punishment and retribution. The meaning is: their account has come to you, and you have known what they did and what was done to them, so remind your people of the Days of Allah (ayyam Allah) and His affairs, glorified is He, and warn them that there may befall them the like of what befell their counterparts.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 19:

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in denial﴾, that is, from your people, ﴿in denial﴾ is a transitional idrab (a turning away from one statement to another; in Arabic grammar, idrab) away from likening them to those [previous peoples], and a clarification that they are worse than them in disbelief and transgression in terms of quantity, as the shift from "yukadhdhibun" (they deny) to ﴿fi takdhib﴾ (in denial) indicates, which conveys that denial encompasses them the way a container encompasses what it contains, or the way the sea encompasses the one drowning in it, along with what its indefiniteness (tankir) conveys of magnifying and emphasizing its enormity. So it is as if it were said: They are not like them; rather they are worse than them, for they are drowned and submerged in a great denial of the Noble Qur'an, so they are more deserving of punishment than them. Or it is as if it were said: Their offence is not merely the failure to take heed and be admonished by what they have heard of its news; rather, along with that, they are in a great denial of the Qur'an that speaks of it, and of its being a Qur'an from Allah, the Exalted, although its matter is clear and its state is manifest through the dazzling proofs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind them﴾ may be taken as an explanatory addition (i'tiraḍ tadhyīlī) [a parenthetical clause that concludes the sense], and it may be taken as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in the preceding prepositional phrase. The statement is a figurative expression (tamthīl) for their inability to escape the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, by the fact that what is encompassed cannot escape the one who encompasses, as many have said. It seems that the meaning is that He, mighty and majestic, knows them and has power over them, and they cannot overpower Him or escape Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He.

ʿIṣām al-Dīn mentioned that in this there is both a rebuke and a reproach for the disbelievers, in that they have cast Allah, glory be to Him, behind their backs and have turned wholly to their desires and appetites. Perhaps this is a shift (ʿudūl) from "their Lord" to "from behind them."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 21:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but it is a glorious Qur'an﴾, is a rejection of their disbelief, a nullification of their denial, and an affirmation of the truth; that is, "Nay, it is a noble Book, of high rank among the divine books in its composition and its meaning, and it is not fitting that it be denied or that one disbelieve in it." It has been said: it is a turning away (idrab) and a transition (intiqal) from informing about the severity of their denial and their failure to desist from it, to describing the Qur'an, to indicate that there is no doubt in it and that the denial of these people does not harm it; but the first is preferable. Some have claimed that the first turning away is from the story of Pharaoh and Thamud to all the disbelievers, and the meaning on this view is that all the disbelievers are in denial, and no Prophet was ever free of their denial, and God Exalted does not neglect their affair; and in this there is some consolation for him, may God bless him and grant him peace, but the following of that by this turning away makes it distant. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "Qur'anu majidin" with the genitive construction (idafa). Ibn Khalawayh said: I heard Ibn al-Anbari say: its meaning is, "Nay, it is the Qur'an of a glorious Lord," just as the poet said:

But for wealth, there is a Lord, Forgiving;

that is, "the wealth of a Forgiving Lord." Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Yamani read it with the genitive construction, so that "the Glorious" is God Exalted, and this is admissible with or without the supposition (of a noun). It is also permitted that it be an idafa of a described noun to its attribute. Abu Hayyan said: this is preferable, because it harmonises the two readings.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 85, verse 22:

﴿In a Tablet﴾ meaning: existing in a Tablet ﴿Preserved﴾ meaning: that Tablet is protected from the reach of the devils. This is the well-known Preserved Tablet, and it is, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and the responsibility for the report rests with the narrator, a tablet of white pearl, whose length is the distance between the heaven and the earth, and whose width is the distance between the east and the west. Its edges are of pearls and rubies, its covers are of red ruby, its pen is light, and it is suspended from the Throne. Its origin lies in the lap of an angel called Satiryun, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, in it, every day, three hundred and sixty glances: He gives life, causes death, grants honour, brings humiliation, and does what He wills. It is also written on its front: "There is no god but Allah, alone, with no partner; His religion is Islam, and Muhammad is His servant and His messenger." Whoever believes in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, affirms His promise, and follows His messengers, He will admit into Paradise. Muqatil said: the Preserved Tablet is to the right of the Throne, and reports other than this have come concerning it. We believe in it, and it is not incumbent upon us to investigate its essence, the manner of its writing, and similar matters. Yes, we say that what some people claim, that it is a pure substance not located in a place, and that it is like a mirror for the lofty forms, contradicts the apparent teachings of the Shari'ah and has no basis in the Book or the Sunnah at all.

Ibn Ya'mur and Ibn as-Sumayfa' read «Luh» with a dammah on the lam. Its original meaning in the language is air, and what is meant here, metaphorically, is what is above the seventh heaven. Al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Muhaysin, and Nafi' in one of the two reports from him read «Mahfuzun» with a raised vowel, as an attribute of the Qur'an, and ﴿in a Tablet﴾ is said to be connected to it, and it is said to be another attribute of the Qur'an.

It has been objected that this involves placing a compound attribute before a single one, which is contrary to the norm, and the meaning according to it is said to be: preserved after its revelation from alteration, substitution, addition and omission, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾. It is also said: preserved in that Tablet from the reach of the devils. And Allah the Exalted knows best.
